title: Glioblastoma in the optic chiasm: A case report
case_prompt: A 77-year-old man presented with a two-month history of progressively worsening bilateral vision loss, more pronounced in the left eye. He was initially diagnosed with non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy and referred for neurology evaluation. He denied headache, mandibular claudication, or pain with eye movements. On examination, pupils were hyporeactive; visual acuity was reduced with dyschromatopsia in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye. No other neurologic deficits were noted. Brain and orbit MRI showed nodular thickening with non-uniform enhancement of the optic chiasm and left optic tract, along with FLAIR hyperintensity in the left mesial temporal lobe and left lateral midbrain. There was no diffusion restriction. Given the possibility of demyelinating disease, oligoclonal bands were sent, and intravenous methylprednisolone was administered, with modest clinical improvement. One month later, he returned with complete bilateral blindness but no new neurologic signs. Repeat contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated progressive thickening and enhancement of the same structures and a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left optic tract.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy was initially suspected because of the patient’s age and painless vision loss — “The initial presumptive diagnosis was a non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy, for which the patient was referred to the emergency room.”  
2. Temporal arteritis was considered but deemed unlikely in the absence of systemic symptoms — “who did not find headache, mandibular claudication, or pain associated with eye movements or in the temporal area.”  
3. Demyelinating optic neuritis was entertained based on MRI findings suggesting inflammation — “These findings suggested an inflammatory compromise or demyelination…”  
4. Neoplastic optic-pathway infiltration remained on the differential because imaging could not exclude a tumor — “…though it was not possible to rule out neoplastic infiltration.”  
5. Demyelinating disease was excluded when follow-up MRI showed progressive nodular enhancement and a discrete mass — “A new brain contrast-enhanced MRI was performed and demonstrated progressive thickening and enhancement of the same structures compared to the previous study and a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left optic tract…”
